---
title: "How do you choose the best plan when everything has a limit?"
subtitle: "You will hunt for the best plan by hand first, then teach a computer to find it. All you need is arithmetic."
engine: knitr
---

A small workshop makes tables and chairs. A table earns \$500 and a chair \$400. So make as many as you can? You can't. A table takes 5 hours on the saw and 2 hours in the paint shop. A chair takes 2 on the saw and 5 in the paint shop. Each week has 30 saw hours and 26 paint hours, and nobody has ordered more than 4 chairs.

How many of each should the workshop make? Most of this guide asks *what will happen?* This lesson asks *what should we do?* A computer can answer that in a blink, but only once someone has written the question down clearly. Writing it down is the part nobody can do for you.

## How many tables and how many chairs?

A plan is two numbers: so many tables, so many chairs. In the picture, a plan is a point. Across is tables, up is chairs, and every faint dot is a plan you could pick.

Drag the ring. The column beside the picture shows what your plan earns, and how many hours it uses on the saw and in the paint shop against the hours there are. A bar that runs past its stop means the plan breaks that limit.

::: {.ink-figure data-figure="plan-workshop" data-step="0" data-caption="Fig. 1 · a made-up workshop: drag your plan and watch the hours"}
:::

Hunt for the best plan you can find. Try 5 tables and 3 chairs first: 5 × 5 + 2 × 3 = 31 saw hours, and there are only 30. Close, but not allowed.

The column keeps your best allowed plan so far. Keep it in mind. A computer will hunt for the same thing in a moment.

Three things decide the answer, and you have just used all of them: **the choices** (how many tables, how many chairs), **the limits** (saw hours, paint hours, orders), and **the goal** (as much profit as possible).

## Which plans are allowed?

Hunting point by point is slow. You can draw the limits instead.

Take the saw. Six tables and no chairs use 6 × 5 = 30 hours, exactly what there is. So does 4 tables and 5 chairs: 20 + 10 = 30. Every plan that uses exactly 30 saw hours sits on one straight line. On one side of it the saw has hours to spare. On the other side it runs out.

Press *draw the next limit* three times. Each limit arrives as a line, with the side that breaks it hatched.

::: {.ink-figure data-figure="plan-workshop" data-step="1" data-caption="Fig. 2 · each limit cuts off the plans that break it"}
:::

The plans nobody hatched are the allowed ones. There is one more limit you never had to draw: you cannot make fewer than zero of anything, so every plan stays right of the left edge and above the bottom edge.

Is your best plan from Fig. 1 inside the clear area? It has to be. And now you can see where the good plans are: up and to the right, as far as the limits let you go.

### Now tell a computer

A computer cannot see the picture. It needs the limits as numbers. The cell below fetches the same three limits, the two profits, and the best plan you found in Fig. 1.

Press **Run**. The first time takes a few seconds while Python starts.

::: {.py-cell data-draw="py-plot"}
```python
from page import limits, profits, my_plan     # the workshop above, and your best plan

print("Limits:", limits)
print("Profit for a table, for a chair:", profits)
print("Your best plan:", my_plan)

picture = {"stars": [my_plan], "xlim": (0, 7), "ylim": (0, 6),
           "xlabel": "tables", "ylabel": "chairs"}
```
:::

`print` writes things out. Each limit is four things in a row: its name, the hours one table uses, the hours one chair uses, and the hours there are. The last line leaves a `picture` behind, a small collection of named things to draw. Here that is one ring, where your plan sits.

Next, a check that a plan breaks no limit. By hand you would take each limit in turn, add up the hours the plan uses, and compare with the hours there are.

::: {.ask}
Before you write code for it: how would you check the code is right?

- **Try it on my best plan.** That only tests one answer, and one you expect to be "allowed". Code that says "allowed" to everything would pass.
- **Try 5 tables and 3 chairs.** Yes. You worked that one out by hand: 31 saw hours when there are 30. The code must say no. Try an allowed plan too, so you see it can say yes.
:::

`def` gives a set of steps a name, so you can use them again. `for ... in limits` takes the limits one at a time and gives the four parts of each a name. `if` does the next line only when something is true, and `return` hands back an answer and stops.

::: {.py-cell}
```python
def allowed(plan):
    tables, chairs = plan                              # a plan is two numbers
    for name, per_table, per_chair, available in limits:
        used = per_table * tables + per_chair * chairs  # hours this plan needs
        if used > ____:                                 # more than there is?
            return False                                # then it breaks this limit
    return True                                        # it broke none of them

print(allowed((5, 3)))      # by hand: 31 saw hours of 30, so False
print(allowed((5, 2)))      # 29 saw hours, 20 paint hours, 2 chairs ordered: True
```
::: {.py-solution}
```python
def allowed(plan):
    tables, chairs = plan                              # a plan is two numbers
    for name, per_table, per_chair, available in limits:
        used = per_table * tables + per_chair * chairs  # hours this plan needs
        if used > available:                            # more than there is?
            return False                                # then it breaks this limit
    return True                                        # it broke none of them

print(allowed((5, 3)))      # by hand: 31 saw hours of 30, so False
print(allowed((5, 2)))      # 29 saw hours, 20 paint hours, 2 chairs ordered: True
```
:::
:::

The orders limit fits the same pattern: a table uses none of it, a chair uses one, and there are 4.

The profit is plainer still. `profits[0]` is the first number in the list, what a table earns, and `profits[1]` is the second.

::: {.py-cell}
```python
def profit(plan):
    tables, chairs = plan
    return profits[0] * tables + ____

print(profit((5, 2)))       # by hand: 2500 + 800 = 3300
print(profit(my_plan))      # compare with your best in Fig. 1
```
::: {.py-solution}
```python
def profit(plan):
    tables, chairs = plan
    return profits[0] * tables + profits[1] * chairs

print(profit((5, 2)))       # by hand: 2500 + 800 = 3300
print(profit(my_plan))      # compare with your best in Fig. 1
```
:::
:::

## Which allowed plan earns the most?

The workshop can make 0 to 7 tables and 0 to 6 chairs, so there are 8 × 7 = 56 plans on the page. A computer does not get bored. It can try all of them.

`range(8)` counts 0, 1, 2 and so on up to 7. A `for` inside another `for` is two loops: for each number of tables, try every number of chairs. `plans` is a list, written with square brackets, and `append` adds one thing to its end.

::: {.py-cell data-draw="py-plot"}
```python
plans = []                          # every plan on the page
for tables in range(8):             # 0 to 7 tables
    for chairs in range(7):         # and, for each, 0 to 6 chairs
        plans.append((tables, chairs))

shapes = []                         # 0 draws a ring, 2 draws a cross
for plan in plans:
    if allowed(plan):
        shapes.append(0)
    else:
        shapes.append(2)

print(len(plans), "plans,", shapes.count(0), "of them allowed")   # count the 0s

picture = {"points": plans, "labels": shapes, "xlim": (-0.5, 7.5), "ylim": (-0.5, 6.5),
           "xlabel": "tables", "ylabel": "chairs",
           "notes": ["ring: allowed", "cross: breaks a limit"]}
```
:::

The rings make the same shape as the clear area in Fig. 2. Your code found the allowed plans one at a time, with no picture to look at.

Now keep the best. By hand you would remember the best allowed plan so far, and swap it out whenever you met a better one. That is what the column in Fig. 1 did while you dragged. Every time the code finds a new best, it saves a picture, so you can watch the ring jump.

::: {.py-cell data-draw="py-plot"}
```python
best = None                         # no plan yet
best_profit = -1                    # so the first allowed plan beats it
frames = []                         # one picture for every new best

for tables in range(8):
    for chairs in range(7):
        plan = (tables, chairs)
        if allowed(plan) and profit(plan) > ____:
            best = plan
            best_profit = profit(plan)
            frames.append({"points": plans, "labels": shapes, "stars": [best],
                           "xlim": (-0.5, 7.5), "ylim": (-0.5, 6.5),
                           "xlabel": "tables", "ylabel": "chairs",
                           "notes": ["best so far " + str(best), "profit $" + str(best_profit)]})

print("Best plan:", best, "Profit:", best_profit)
print("Yours:", my_plan, "Profit:", profit(my_plan))
```
::: {.py-solution}
```python
best = None                         # no plan yet
best_profit = -1                    # so the first allowed plan beats it
frames = []                         # one picture for every new best

for tables in range(8):
    for chairs in range(7):
        plan = (tables, chairs)
        if allowed(plan) and profit(plan) > best_profit:
            best = plan
            best_profit = profit(plan)
            frames.append({"points": plans, "labels": shapes, "stars": [best],
                           "xlim": (-0.5, 7.5), "ylim": (-0.5, 6.5),
                           "xlabel": "tables", "ylabel": "chairs",
                           "notes": ["best so far " + str(best), "profit $" + str(best_profit)]})

print("Best plan:", best, "Profit:", best_profit)
print("Yours:", my_plan, "Profit:", profit(my_plan))
```
:::
:::

`and` means both must be true: the plan is allowed, and it earns more than the best so far. `str` turns a plan into text, so it can go in a note. The code settles on 5 tables and 2 chairs, for \$3,300. Compare it with the best you found in Fig. 1. If you found the same plan, you did by hand exactly what the loops did.

## Where is the best plan?

Fifty-six plans is nothing for a computer. A real factory chooses hundreds of amounts at once, and there are far too many combinations to try them all. You need to know where to look.

For a moment, forget whole numbers. Pretend the workshop can make part of a table this week and finish it next week. Then every point in the clear area is a plan, not just the dots.

::: {.ask data-veil="true"}
Where would the plan with the most profit be?

- **Somewhere in the middle of the allowed area.** Pick any plan in the middle. Add a little more of either: still allowed, and richer. So the middle can always be beaten.
- **On its edge, against a limit.** Yes, it must be: anywhere else you could add a little more of something. But an edge is long. Which point on it?
- **At a corner.** That is the claim. Slide the line and see if it holds.
:::

Every plan that earns exactly \$1,500 sits on one straight line: 3 tables, or 3¾ chairs, or anything between. Every plan that earns \$3,000 sits on another line, parallel to the first and further out. Drag the slider to move the line, or press *push it out*.

::: {.ink-figure data-figure="plan-workshop" data-step="2" data-caption="Fig. 3 · a line of equal profit, pushed out until it is about to leave"}
:::

For a while the line still crosses the allowed area, so that profit can be reached. Then it is about to leave, and the last plan it touches is a corner. That is the best plan: 4⅔ tables and 3⅓ chairs, for \$3,667, exactly where the saw line and the paint line cross. At that corner both are used up, to the hour.

So you only ever need to check the corners. Here there are five. Work one by hand: at 3 tables and 4 chairs the profit is 1500 + 1600 = 3100.

::: {.py-cell data-draw="py-plot"}
```python
corners = [(0, 0), (6, 0), (14 / 3, 10 / 3), (3, 4), (0, 4)]   # around the allowed area

top = corners[0]
for c in corners:
    print("corner", (round(c[0], 2), round(c[1], 2)), "profit", round(profit(c)))
    if profit(c) > profit(top):
        top = c

print("Best corner:", (round(top[0], 2), round(top[1], 2)), "Profit:", round(profit(top)))

picture = {"lines": [corners + [corners[0]]],      # the outline, back to the start
           "points": corners, "stars": [top],
           "xlim": (-0.5, 7.5), "ylim": (-0.5, 6.5), "xlabel": "tables", "ylabel": "chairs",
           "notes": ["5 corners checked", "not 56 plans"]}
```
:::

`round(x, 2)` keeps two figures after the point, so 4.666… prints as 4.67. Compare the printed profits with the list in Fig. 3: they are the same five numbers.

Why a corner? Walk along any edge of the area and the profit changes steadily, always up or always down, because it is just so much per table plus so much per chair. So you can always do at least as well by walking on to the corner at the end. This gives a fast method even for thousands of choices: start at one corner, step to a neighbouring corner that earns more, and stop when none does. If the line happens to lie exactly along an edge, every plan on that edge ties, and a corner is still among the best.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="The same thing in symbols"}
Write $x_1$ for the number of tables and $x_2$ for the number of chairs. The whole workshop is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{maximise} \quad & 500 x_1 + 400 x_2 \\
\text{subject to} \quad & 5 x_1 + 2 x_2 \le 30 \quad (\text{saw}) \\
& 2 x_1 + 5 x_2 \le 26 \quad (\text{paint}) \\
& x_2 \le 4 \quad (\text{orders}) \\
& x_1, x_2 \ge 0
\end{aligned}
$$

Read $\le$ as "at most" and $\ge$ as "at least". The best corner is where the saw and paint lines cross, where both hold exactly: $5x_1 + 2x_2 = 30$ and $2x_1 + 5x_2 = 26$. Multiply the first by 5 and the second by 2 to get $25x_1 + 10x_2 = 150$ and $4x_1 + 10x_2 = 52$. Take one from the other: $21x_1 = 98$, so $x_1 = 14/3 \approx 4.67$, and then $x_2 = 10/3 \approx 3.33$.
:::

## What if you can only make whole tables?

Nobody buys two thirds of a table. The obvious fix is to round the best corner: 4.67 tables becomes 5, and 3.33 chairs becomes 3. `round` with no second number rounds to a whole number.

This cell also checks the plan before it would be sent to the workshop floor. `assert` means: stop right here if this is not true.

::: {.py-cell data-aside="true"}
```python
best_corner = (14 / 3, 10 / 3)
rounded = (round(best_corner[0]), round(best_corner[1]))   # 4.67 -> 5, 3.33 -> 3
print("Rounded plan:", rounded, "Profit:", profit(rounded))

for name, per_table, per_chair, available in limits:
    print(name, per_table * rounded[0] + per_chair * rounded[1], "of", available)

assert allowed(rounded), "the rounded plan breaks a limit"
```
:::

It stops with `AssertionError`. The rounded plan needs 31 saw hours, and there are 30. You saw the same thing in Fig. 1 when you tried 5 and 3. The best corner was right on the saw line, so nudging it outward stepped over the line.

::: {.ask}
So what should the workshop make?

- **Round down instead: 4 tables, 3 chairs.** That is allowed, and earns \$3,200. But your loops found 5 and 2, which earns \$3,300. Rounding down is safe, not best.
- **Look at the whole plans next to the corner.** Here that works: 5 and 2 is close by. Now set a table to \$900 in Fig. 4. The corner does not move, but the best whole plan jumps all the way to 6 tables and no chairs.
- **Try every whole plan.** That is what your two loops did, and it is the only one of these that is always right. It works for 56 plans. It does not work for millions.
:::

::: {.ink-figure data-figure="plan-workshop" data-step="3" data-caption="Fig. 4 · the best corner, its rounding, and the best whole plan, checked one by one"}
:::

Slide what a table earns. The corner jumps from one place to another, and the best whole plan wanders on its own, sometimes next to the corner, sometimes nowhere near it. With whole numbers the best plan is usually not at a corner of the area, so the trick of checking corners stops working. Whole-number problems are genuinely harder. Small ones are fine. Some quite small ones still have no known best answer after days of computing.

## What goes wrong when you write it down?

Every problem like this has the same three parts: the choices, the limits, and the goal. Writing them down clearly is most of the work, and it is where mistakes happen.

**The same three parts, upside down.** A meal must have at least 8 g of protein and at least 10 g of carbohydrate. A serving of bread has 2 g of protein, 4 g of carbohydrate and costs \$0.20. A serving of cheese has 5 g, 1 g and \$0.50. The choices: servings of bread, servings of cheese. The limits: at least 8 g of protein, at least 10 g of carbohydrate. The goal: as *little* cost as possible. Its best plan is 2⅓ servings of bread and ⅔ of cheese, for \$0.80. All bread, 4 servings, also costs \$0.80: here the cost line lies exactly along the protein edge, so that whole edge ties. A problem very like this one, feeding soldiers as cheaply as possible, is where this whole subject began in the 1940s.

**Choosing the choices.** A call centre needs a certain number of people each day of the week. Everyone works 5 days in a row, then has 2 days off.

::: {.ask}
What should the choices be?

- **How many people work on each day.** The natural guess. The days are easy to write. But "5 in a row, then 2 off" is very hard to say in these numbers: nothing stops Monday having 10 people and Tuesday 30 different ones.
- **How many people start their five days on each day.** Yes. Tuesday's crew is then everyone who started on Friday, Saturday, Sunday, Monday or Tuesday, and those five numbers added up must reach Tuesday's need. The "5 in a row" rule is built into what each number means, so it never has to be written as a limit.
:::

When a limit is awkward to write, ask whether different choices would make it disappear.

**Yes-or-no choices.** Some choices are not amounts. Build the factory or not. Buy this stock or not. Write such a choice as a number that can only be 0 (no) or 1 (yes), and plain arithmetic can say a lot:

| What you want | What you write |
|:--|:--|
| Must buy Tesla | Tesla's number = 1 |
| At least one of Amazon, Google, Apple | their three numbers add up to at least 1 |
| Exactly one of them | their three numbers add up to exactly 1 |
| FedEx and UPS together, or neither | FedEx's number = UPS's number |
| Coke or Pepsi, but not both and not neither | Coke's number = 1 − Pepsi's number |

A yes-or-no number can also be tied to an amount. Say you can put up to \$100,000 into a stock. Write "amount ≤ 100,000 × yes-or-no". If the answer is no (0), the amount must be 0; if yes (1), it can be anything up to the budget. A minimum works the same way: "amount ≥ 5,000 × yes-or-no" means you buy nothing or at least \$5,000. A flat fee for buying a stock at all is "fee × yes-or-no", added to the cost.

Tie them together yourself. The computer only sees the numbers you wrote, not what you meant. If you never wrote the rule that ties an amount to its yes-or-no, the computer will happily invest money in a stock it said no to.

Yes-or-no numbers are whole numbers, so they bring back the trouble from the last section. Use them when you need them, not by habit.

**When the numbers are guesses.** Everything here treated 30 saw hours and 4 chair orders as certain. Real numbers are forecasts, and a plan that is best for the forecast can be terrible when the forecast is off. There are four common answers: leave a safety margin in the limits; ask for a limit to hold most of the time, say 95% of the time; write down several possible futures and find a plan that works in all of them, or is best on average across them; or plan one step at a time, deciding again as each future unfolds.

## Where have you seen this before?

Several earlier lessons were this all along. Fitting a straight line through points chose two numbers, the tilt and the height, to make the total squared miss as small as possible. The choices were the tilt and the height; there were no limits; the goal was the smallest miss. Moving flags to the middle of their dots made a total as small as possible too. So does almost every model in this guide.

One word will trip you up. A statistician calls the columns of the data "variables", because they vary from row to row. Someone solving problems like this one calls the *choices* "variables", because they are what the computer varies. When you fit a line, those are the tilt and the height. Check which meaning someone has in mind.

And because fitting is choosing, you can change the rules: force the line through zero, or measure the miss differently. A ready-made fitting function will not let you. A general solver will.

## What you just built

Everything you did has a name:

| What you did | What it is called |
|:--|:--|
| Choosing what to do, not predicting what will happen | Optimisation (prescriptive analytics) |
| The choices: how many tables, how many chairs | Decision variables |
| The limits | Constraints |
| The goal: as much profit as possible | Objective function |
| A plan that breaks no limit | A feasible solution |
| All of the allowed plans, the clear area | The feasible region |
| The allowed plan that earns the most | The optimal solution |
| A line of equal profit | An iso-profit line (a level line of the objective) |
| A limit that is used up exactly at the best plan | A binding constraint; the others have slack |
| Straight-line goal and limits, any amounts | A linear program |
| Walking from corner to better corner | The simplex method |
| Whole numbers only | An integer program |
| Yes-or-no numbers, 0 or 1 | Binary variables |
| Leave a margin; hold most of the time; several futures; decide step by step | Conservative constraints; chance constraints; scenario optimisation; dynamic programming (Markov decision processes) |

A best plan is either optimal or it is not; "more optimal" means nothing, like "more best".

Problems come in kinds, from easy to hard. Linear programs solve in moments even with millions of choices. Problems shaped like a network (shortest routes, matching people to jobs) are faster still. Bending the goal into a smooth bowl, as in fitting a line, is still quick. Whole numbers are hard. Goals with many separate dips and peaks can be hopeless even when small. The same problem, written two ways, can land in different kinds, so the writing matters more than the solver.

Libraries do the solving: SciPy's `linprog` in Python, or `lpSolve` in R as below. You hand them the profits, the hours each choice uses and the hours there are. They walk the corners for you, and for whole-number problems they search far more cleverly than your loops. Writing down the three parts is still your job.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Reference: the same ideas in R"}
Every result below is produced by the R on this page. Open "The R" under any of them to see the code.

The diet problem, solved with `lpSolve`: the objective, the constraint matrix, the directions and the right-hand sides.

```{r}
#| label: lp-solve

library(lpSolve)

# Objective: minimize 0.20 x1 + 0.50 x2
objective <- c(0.20, 0.50)

# Constraints: LHS coefficients, directions, RHS
constraints <- matrix(c(
  2, 5,   # protein
  4, 1    # carbs
), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)

directions <- c(">=", ">=")
rhs        <- c(8, 10)

sol <- lp(direction    = "min",
          objective.in = objective,
          const.mat    = constraints,
          const.dir    = directions,
          const.rhs    = rhs)

cat("Optimal cost:       $", round(sol$objval, 3), "\n")
cat("Bread servings x1:  ", round(sol$solution[1], 3), "\n")
cat("Cheese servings x2: ", round(sol$solution[2], 3), "\n")
```

The feasible region for the diet problem, with the optimum and one iso-cost line through it.

```{r}
#| label: plot-feasible
#| fig-cap: "Feasible region for the diet LP. Each constraint cuts off a half-plane; the feasible set is their intersection. The optimum of a linear objective lives at a vertex of this region."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 6

par(mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))
plot(NULL, xlim = c(0, 6), ylim = c(0, 6),
     xlab = expression(x[1] * " (bread)"),
     ylab = expression(x[2] * " (cheese)"),
     main = "Feasible region for the diet LP")
abline(h = 0, v = 0, col = "gray85")
grid()

# Protein: 2 x1 + 5 x2 = 8  ->  x2 = (8 - 2 x1) / 5
x1_seq <- seq(0, 6, length.out = 200)
lines(x1_seq, (8 - 2 * x1_seq) / 5, col = "#d62828", lwd = 2)
text(5.3, (8 - 2 * 5.3) / 5 - 0.25, "protein", col = "#d62828", cex = 0.9)

# Carbs:   4 x1 + 1 x2 = 10 ->  x2 = 10 - 4 x1
lines(x1_seq, 10 - 4 * x1_seq, col = "#1f4e79", lwd = 2)
text(1.1, 10 - 4 * 1.1 + 0.3, "carbs", col = "#1f4e79", cex = 0.9)

# Shade feasible region (above both lines and in the positive quadrant)
grid_points <- expand.grid(x1 = seq(0, 6, 0.05), x2 = seq(0, 6, 0.05))
feasible <- with(grid_points,
                 2 * x1 + 5 * x2 >= 8 &
                 4 * x1 + 1 * x2 >= 10 &
                 x1 >= 0 & x2 >= 0)
points(grid_points[feasible, ], col = adjustcolor("#2d6a4f", 0.15),
       pch = 15, cex = 0.4)

# Mark the optimal solution
points(sol$solution[1], sol$solution[2], pch = 19, col = "#6c00a3", cex = 1.8)
text(sol$solution[1] + 0.2, sol$solution[2] + 0.3,
     sprintf("optimum\n(%.2f, %.2f)", sol$solution[1], sol$solution[2]),
     col = "#6c00a3", cex = 0.85, adj = 0)

# Show one iso-cost line at the optimum for the direction
iso_level <- sol$objval
lines(x1_seq, (iso_level - 0.20 * x1_seq) / 0.50,
      col = "gray40", lty = 3)
text(4.8, (iso_level - 0.20 * 4.8) / 0.50 + 0.2,
     "iso-cost line", col = "gray40", cex = 0.8)

legend("topright",
       legend = c("protein constraint", "carbs constraint",
                  "feasible region", "optimum"),
       col = c("#d62828", "#1f4e79",
               adjustcolor("#2d6a4f", 0.4), "#6c00a3"),
       lty = c(1, 1, NA, NA), pch = c(NA, NA, 15, 19),
       lwd = c(2, 2, NA, NA), bty = "n", cex = 0.85)
```

The call centre, with one variable for each start day. The 5-in-a-row rule lives in the coverage matrix, not in any constraint.

```{r}
#| label: call-center

days <- c("Mon", "Tue", "Wed", "Thu", "Fri", "Sat", "Sun")

# Demand forecast
demand <- c(Mon = 17, Tue = 13, Wed = 15, Thu = 19, Fri = 14, Sat = 16, Sun = 11)

# Variables: x[i] = workers starting their 5-day stretch on day i
# Each x[i] covers 5 consecutive days starting at i (wrapping around the week)

# Build the coverage matrix: rows = days of demand, cols = start days
n_days <- 7
coverage <- matrix(0, nrow = n_days, ncol = n_days)
for (start in 1:n_days) {
  covered <- ((start - 1) + 0:4) %% n_days + 1
  coverage[covered, start] <- 1
}
dimnames(coverage) <- list(day_of_demand = days, start_day = days)
coverage

# Solve: minimize sum of workers hired, subject to coverage >= demand
lp_sched <- lp(
  direction    = "min",
  objective.in = rep(1, n_days),
  const.mat    = coverage,
  const.dir    = rep(">=", n_days),
  const.rhs    = demand,
  all.int      = TRUE
)

cat("Total workers needed:", lp_sched$objval, "\n\n")
cat("Workers starting each day:\n")
schedule <- setNames(lp_sched$solution, days)
print(schedule)

cat("\nCoverage per day (must be >= demand):\n")
coverage_actual <- as.vector(coverage %*% lp_sched$solution)
print(setNames(coverage_actual, days))
```

A small portfolio with a budget, a fixed fee and a minimum per stock, at least one of AMZN, GOOG and AAPL, and FedEx and UPS as a matched pair. The solver picks the best set, respects the minimum-investment rule, includes at least one of {AMZN, GOOG, AAPL}, and treats FedEx/UPS as a matched pair.

```{r}
#| label: portfolio-binary

stocks <- c("TSLA", "AMZN", "GOOG", "AAPL", "FDX", "UPS")
returns <- c(0.18, 0.15, 0.12, 0.14, 0.09, 0.08)  # expected return (decimal)
budget <- 100000
min_invest <- 5000      # can't invest less than $5k per stock
txn_fee <- 150           # fixed fee per stock we pick

# Decision variables: x1..x6 (dollars in each) then y1..y6 (binary pick)
# Maximize: sum(returns * x) - sum(txn_fee * y)
# Equivalently: minimize -(sum(returns * x) - sum(txn_fee * y))
n <- length(stocks)
objective <- c(-returns, rep(txn_fee, n))  # minimize

# Constraints:
# 1. Budget:              sum(x_i) <= budget
# 2. Linking (upper):     x_i - budget * y_i <= 0    for each i
# 3. Linking (lower min): x_i - min_invest * y_i >= 0 for each i
# 4. At least one of {AMZN, GOOG, AAPL}: y_AMZN + y_GOOG + y_AAPL >= 1
# 5. FedEx/UPS both or neither: y_FDX - y_UPS = 0

# Budget row
A <- rbind(c(rep(1, n), rep(0, n)))
dir <- c("<=")
rhs <- c(budget)

# Linking constraints
for (i in 1:n) {
  row_upper <- rep(0, 2 * n)
  row_upper[i] <- 1
  row_upper[n + i] <- -budget
  A <- rbind(A, row_upper); dir <- c(dir, "<="); rhs <- c(rhs, 0)

  row_lower <- rep(0, 2 * n)
  row_lower[i] <- 1
  row_lower[n + i] <- -min_invest
  A <- rbind(A, row_lower); dir <- c(dir, ">="); rhs <- c(rhs, 0)
}

# At least one of AMZN (2), GOOG (3), AAPL (4)
one_of <- rep(0, 2 * n)
one_of[n + 2] <- 1; one_of[n + 3] <- 1; one_of[n + 4] <- 1
A <- rbind(A, one_of); dir <- c(dir, ">="); rhs <- c(rhs, 1)

# FDX (5) == UPS (6)
both_or_neither <- rep(0, 2 * n)
both_or_neither[n + 5] <- 1
both_or_neither[n + 6] <- -1
A <- rbind(A, both_or_neither); dir <- c(dir, "="); rhs <- c(rhs, 0)

sol_port <- lp(
  direction    = "min",
  objective.in = objective,
  const.mat    = A,
  const.dir    = dir,
  const.rhs    = rhs,
  int.vec      = (n + 1):(2 * n),          # y_i are integer
  binary.vec   = (n + 1):(2 * n)           # and binary
)

x_vals <- sol_port$solution[1:n]
y_vals <- sol_port$solution[(n + 1):(2 * n)]

portfolio <- data.frame(
  stock    = stocks,
  picked   = as.logical(y_vals),
  invested = round(x_vals, 0),
  expected_return = round(x_vals * returns, 0)
)
portfolio

cat("\nTotal invested: $", sum(x_vals), "\n")
cat("Expected return net of fees: $",
    round(sum(x_vals * returns) - sum(y_vals * txn_fee), 0), "\n")
```

Linear regression twice: once with `lm()`, once by handing the sum of squared errors to `optim()`.

```{r}
#| label: regression-as-optim

set.seed(42)
n <- 60
x <- runif(n, 0, 10)
y <- 2 + 1.5 * x + rnorm(n, 0, 1)

# Standard lm
fit_lm <- lm(y ~ x)
cat("lm() intercept =",    round(coef(fit_lm)[1], 4),
    "   slope =",          round(coef(fit_lm)[2], 4), "\n")

# As an optimization problem: minimize sum((y - a0 - a1*x)^2) over (a0, a1)
sse <- function(params) {
  a0 <- params[1]; a1 <- params[2]
  sum((y - a0 - a1 * x)^2)
}

fit_optim <- optim(par = c(0, 0), fn = sse, method = "BFGS")
cat("optim() intercept =", round(fit_optim$par[1], 4),
    "   slope =",          round(fit_optim$par[2], 4), "\n")
```
:::
